speakeroldname: Hon. ERNEST LAPOINTE (Minister of Justice) moved:
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: APPOINTMENT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER QUESTION
speechtext:
That a special committee consisting of fifteen members to be selected at a later date be appointed to consider the question of the adequacy of the remuneration paid to the judges of the various courts in Canada, and all matters pertaining thereto, with power to call for persons, papers and records, to examine witnesses under oath, and to report from time to time.
He said: Mr. Speaker, during recent years legal associations and other bodies have passed resolutions asking parliament to consider the remuneration; of judges. Those resolutions have been received from time to time and the matter has been referred to incidentally, especially during last session. Since then the Canadian Bar Association has taken formal action and adopted certain resolutions, which have been submitted to the government by a committee of the association. As Minister of Justice I have been receiving resolutions from the law associations of every province with regard to this matter. Moreover, a committee of various county court judges is to meet the government in support of the claim that they have submitted for higher remuneration. We promised at the time that the matter would be called to the attention of parliament for consideration and study. I believe that inasmuch as the judges are servants of the people and therefore more properly servants of parliament rather than of the government the question should be considered by parliament, and I do not see any better way of dealing with it than by the appointment of a special committee for the purpose.

speakeroldname: Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Leader of the Opposition) :
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: APPOINTMENT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER QUESTION
speechtext:
I greatly regret that I am entirely opposed to the appointment of a committee to deal with this matter. As I explained to the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) on a previous occasion, I am wholly in accord with the idea of increasing the salaries of judges in this country. I have so stated publicly, and I was one of those who constituted a committee to wait upon the government as representing the Canadian Bar Association. I have long taken the view that if we are to command for the public service as judges the best men in the legal profession we must pay them salaries commensurate with the dignity and the responsibility of the position they hold. But I cannot agree with the appointment of a committee to examine witnesses under oath and to send for papers and' persons; I do not believe that this would serve the

purpose intended. The appointment of a committee would be, in my opinion, fraught with the gravest possibilities of disaster to the whole project. Moreover, it is not the method that should be followed in dealing with a matter of this kind. All that is necessary is to amend the Judges Act. All that is essential to accomplish the object which the government has in view is for the minister to bring in the necessary measure-because obviously the opposition cannot introduce a bill involving the payment of moneys from the public exchequer-and I venture to say that most of those who sit on this side will be glad to give it their support. But to appoint a committee at this time is in my opinion not only wrong; it Shifts responsibility and' makes it impossible to deal with the question as it should be dealt with. I cannot think that the calling of witnesses, the bringing of papers, and a general discussion in a select committee of this house would be anything but injurious to the very purpose we hope to accomplish; and I can only say on behalf of myself and of those associated with me-

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: APPOINTMENT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER QUESTION
speechtext: Will my hon. friend indicate in what way the consideration of the question by a committee of parliament might be injurious to the object in view?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: APPOINTMENT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER QUESTION
speechtext:
The very bringing of
papers and the examination of witnesses, as suggested in the motion, would bring about such discussions as would, in my judgment, render it impossible in the end to carry into effect the purpose which the minister desires to achieve. That is my view. I may be altogether wrong, and I am only expressing my own opinion, as I did to my hon. friend the other day. It seems to me that the Minister of Justice should introduce a bill to amend the Judges Act, increasing the present salaries of the judges by such an amount as in his opinion, and in the opinion of the executive of the country, the cabinet, would be a reasonable addition to the stipends they now receive. Certainly most of those associated with me on this side would be glad to support such a measure. That is the only position I can take.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER QUESTION
speechtext:
May I ask the
leader of the opposition whether he implies that this is a matter that will not stand investigation?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: APPOINTMENT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER QUESTION
speechtext:
Had that observation
come from anyone less educated than my hon. friend I would treat it with contempt. The hon. member is perfectly well aware that the judges of this country 'are discharging by all odds the gravest, the most serious and

the most difficult duties with which men can be charged in a free country, and it is essential that the compensation paid them for the services they render should be at least consistent with the obligations that are imposed upon them, as well as with the dignity of the position they hold. Any investigation that might be held in this house certainly would not disclose any facts other than these, while on the other hand much extraneous matter would be dragged in. The result would be that instead of the committee being able to focus its attention upon the one point that would be considered in this house in committee on a bill for the purpose, a great deal of irrelevant discussion would ensue with respect to whether John Smith might not be able to live cheaper, whether John Jones was receiving enough to cope with the high cost of living, or whether he ought to keep an automobile or a pair of horses. For these reasons I am opposed to the motion.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: APPOINTMENT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER QUESTION
speechtext:
On different occasions we
have heard in this chamber the suggestion that the government, in respect of measures of this kind, should seek to take parliament more into its confidence before bringing down legislation. We felt that in this particular instance there was strong ground for acting upon that suggestion. If all of us were members of the legal profession, as are my hon. friend and the Minister of Justice, we should have no difficulty in appreciating fully the reasons that make it all-important that the judiciary in this country should be well paid. But we are not all in that position, and there are some hon. members of the house, and many persons throughout the country as well, who find it difficult to appreciate the reasons why members of the judiciary should receive not only increases in their salaries but the salaries which at the present time they are actually being paid. The government believes that if a committee were appointed representative of all groups in the house and occasion afforded to interested parties to appear and submit their views, the probable result will be that an agreement will be reached whereby the house will be saved a controversy which might be unduly protracted and might in some other respects be unfortunate. For these reasons, and following to some extent a parallel method of procedure-I will not call it a precedent-which has been adopted elsewhere, we have thought it advisable to suggest the appointment of a committee. The United States congress last year, I am informed, had under consideration a proposal to increase the salaries of judges.
Preceding the discussion of the question in congress a committee was appointed before whom representations were made by interested' parties. The result there was apparently satisfactory to the administration in meeting just the kind of difficulties I have indicated may arise. The government considering, as I have said, the frequent expression of the view that some of these matters involving executive action might be proceeded with the better, if in the first instance hon. members were taken more largely into its confidence, deemed it advisable to have a special committee appointed for the purpose.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER QUESTION
speechtext: With reference to the points mentioned by the Prime Minister, does he not think that the proposed method of procedure is putting the judges in a very undignified position? Why have them come as suppliants before a committee of parliament on a question which parliament, of its own volition, should consider without the unpleasant discussion which would be inevitable if a committee were appointed to investigate the matter? Would it not be better for the government to formulate and submit a measure, and have it discussed in this house? That would be much more dignified and would place our judiciary in a more desirable position.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: APPOINTMENT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER QUESTION
speechtext:
No one suggests that
the members of the high courts of the land should come here as suppliants. No one wants them to do so. The bar may be represented in the committee. In the committee which considered a similar question before congress in the United States former Secretary of State, Mr. Hughes, came and addressed its members, the president of the American Federation of Labour, Mr. Green, supported the request, and Mr. Lewis, the president of the United Mine Workers also appeared. Various interests were represented. I do not suggest, and no one does, that the judges themselves should come in the capacity indicated by my hon. friend. But what would be the harm in a committee considering the question and inquiring into salaries paid in the various dominions of the empire as well as in foreign countries, and making comparisons, bearing upon the cost of living, with the salaries paid in other professions? I think this is a proper matter for investigation; there is nothing unworthy or undignified in it, and I believe it is the only way properly to deal with the matter. If everyone would help instead of criticising a point of procedure I think we would more speedily come to a satisfactory conclusion.

speechtext:
I cannot agree with my right hon.
friend the Prime Minister in the .precedent which he has cited for the present procedure, or with the proposal for *1316 appointment of a committee of this house to consider the question of the salaries of our judges. The judicial system in the United States is entirely different from the judicial system of this country; it has little relation to the system which we enjoy in Canada. Futhermore the legislative and administrative system in congress is very different from the system adopted in this parliament. In Canada it has been a usage, and indeed a law, that all measures involving public expenditure shall be initiated by the government of the country; in congress the system is entirely different. There it is done by a committee on appropriations, called by some a committee on the budget. In every instance in this country, however, by the rules of procedure and by the usage of parliament, when a public expenditure is proposed! the government of the day must accept the full responsibility.
During the last twenty-five or thirty years the salaries of our judges have been increased on several occasions by this house, and it has always been done 'by amendments to the Judges Act. That is the constitutional procedure. The government have all the information in their files with regard to the salaries received by judges in other countries; that information has been there for a long time, having been carefully gathered by the bar associations and placed in the hands of the Minister of Justice. He has every facility for knowing what should properly be paid to those high officials in this country. The cabinet should formulate their scheme, if they think the salaries paid! to-day are too low; let them take the bold course and announce what they think should be paid. Do not let this question of judicial salaries go before a special committee, where evidence of all kinds will be given and where the discussion will probably degenerate into a consideration of the high cost of living or something of that kind. We have had committees of that sort in this parliament, one of which I remember particularly. A committee on the high cost of living sat for about three months in 1919, I believe, and we all know the utter lack of result in their work. In this case, the parties most interested in the result, the judges themselves, are the very people who Should (not be called. Why does not the government take the parliamentary course, the bold course, and formulate their plan, decide what they think should properly be paid to the judges of this

country, and bring it before parliament? They have all the information before them, and after the second reading of the bill, and when the house goas into committee, the fullest information can be placed at the disposal of parliament. Surely such is the course which should be pursued in this instance. Personally I favour reasonable increases in judicial salaries. I have heard it rumoured that on the government side there is anything but unanimity on this question, and that as a solution of the difficulty in which the government find themselves this committee is proposed. I do not believe we should depart from well-known. parliamentary procedure simply on account of some difference of opinion in the government ranks upon this very important question.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
subtopic: APPOINTMENT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER QUESTION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I wish to say just one word in answer to my hon. friend. When he said that in the United States the initiation of legislation which meant the expenditure of public money was in the hands of congress and not in the hands of the executive government, whereas the rule in Canada is different since the executive must take the initiative in all legislation involving the expenditure of public money, he was perfectly correct. In this matter, however, considering its importance, the government think that parliament, through a committee, should inquire into the whole subject, secure the requisite information and report to the house. Then, when that report is made, the government will introduce legislation accordingly, if legislation be necessary. I do not think this is a matter which should be treated in a partisan or political way at all.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER QUESTION
speechtext: Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
subtopic: APPOINTMENT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER QUESTION

If my hon. friends opposite wish to help the administration of justice in Canada, do they consider they are doing so by adopting the narrow stand which they now take in the house? If the salaries of our judges are to be increased, let us treat this matter in an open, frank and sincere fashion. When my hon. friends siay it would be undignified to have such a parliamentary committee, they seem to forget that after all this parliament of ours is the highest court of justice in Canada, and that whether we sit as a House of Commons or as a committee of the house of our own appointment, we sit as a tribunal where all matters, including those relative to the salaries of our judges, will always be treated in such a way that the dignity of no one will suffer thereby.

My point in this somewhat disjointed argument is that the traditions of the judiciary itself seem to have influenced those who have been appointed to it so that they measure up to those traditions. It is very desirable in the interest of the country at large that nothing should be done that will bring the judiciary of Canada into the realm of, what shall I say, a wrangle or discussion or dispute about such a thing as salaries. In other words, in days gone by and up to the present the judiciary have trusted parliament to supply a reasonable and sufficient salary for them, and my opinion is that it would be better to leave this subject to parliament rather than to have an investigation.
The Minister of Justice cited the fact that a committee in the United States had been appointed to consider this question and that was offered as a sound precedent for us to follow. If our following the United States in that respect had any danger of inducing us to follow them in their process or method of appointing judges, that is by the two-year elective system, then' heaven save us from following precedents of the United States.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I was referring to federal lourt judges who are not elected but who are appointed by the United States government.
Thousands of judges in be United States are elected every two years.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Those were not dealt with by the committee of congress. They are placed by the various states.

That does not alter my point, if the minister will catch what I am driving at. I do not think a precedent established by the United States congress should govern us in a ease of this kind. Our system of appointing judges, the traditions which surround our judiciary, the reputation and the record of our judges generally, with very few if any exceptions, are so much better than they are on the other side of the line that we should do nothing that would interfere with or jeopardize that very high standard. It is unfair to submit one side of a question to a committee when the other side is not supposed to come, and it would be most unfortunate if the judiciary of Canada were called before a committee of parliament on the question of salaries.

I just want to ask the minister a question. The resolution states:
That a special committee. ... be appointed to consider the question of the adequacy of the remuneration paid to the judges of the various courts in Canada.
In view of the remark of the Solicitor General (Mr. Cannon) that this is the highest court in Canada, I would ask if it is the intention that the committee shall inquire whether the judges in this .particular court are paid high enough salaries or not.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I suppose it will be for
the committee itsblf to decide whether the judges of this court should be included in the salary revision.

I have only one or two observations to make as to why I shall vote against this motion if it comes to a vote. I shall vote against it because I do not propose to assist the government in carrying out obligations which should properly fall upon them. If the government is prepared to say that in the appointment of judges they will consider representations made by members on this side of the house, then I am prepared to join with them in the appointment of a committee to fix the salaries, but I am not prepared to assist them in lifting from their shoulders the burden which should fall upon them by appointing a committee without consideration of the views of anybody else.
I do not concur in the remarks made by the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens), and concurred in by the hon. Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe). The hon. member for Vancouver Centre thinks it would be a terrible thing to have judges come before the committee to give evidlenee or to be questioned. Well, if it is derogatory to the dignity of the judges to come before a committee and give evidence, than it must also be derogatory to their dignity when they make representations in writing to the government and to parliament asking for an increase in their salaries. If it is not lowering to the dignity of judges to make representations in writing to members of parliament for an increase in their salaries, I submit that it is not derogatory to their dignity to appear before a committee and give evidence.
There seems to be an opinion in the mind of the Minister of Justice, concurred in by the hon. member for Vancouver Centre, that we can place these judges in different categories. The hon. member for Vancouver Centre made no classification. He said! that it would be against the dignity of any judge to appear

before a committee and give evidence. Oh no, says the Minister of Justice, I would not go quite that far; I would object, to having the 'higher judges come before the committee to give evidence, but you might bring before the committee the county court judges. Carried to its logical conclusion, that means that in the mind of the Minister of Justice the dignity of a judge is expressed in the salary he draws, and it is not derogatory to the dignity of a judge drawing five or six thousand a year to appear before the committee and give evidence in favour of an increase in his salary, but it is derogatory in the case of a man who is getting a salary of fifteen or sixteen thousand a year, and who will get an even bigger increase than the lower judge. But the higher judge must get his increase without lowering his dignity to the extent of appearing before a committee and telling the reason why he is starving to death on his salary of fifteen thousand a year. I do not exactly see it in that light myself.
There is one other thing in connection with the appointment of this committee. If you are going to appoint a committee to consider this matter, in the first place I say let the government take the full responsibility for appointing the committee. In the second place, I submit that there should not be one single lawyer on that committee-not one. My regard for them is so extremely high and my love for them so great that I would not for the life of me stand here and permit them so to jeopardize their dignity, or the dignity of the position they may ultimately occupy. In the third place, I would warn the government, for very obvious reasons, against appointing to that committee the hon. Minister of Justice, and certainly they should not appoint to that committee the Solicitor General (Mr. Cannon), the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Cardin), or the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Elliott). None of these gentlemen should be appointed to that committee because it would always leave them open to the reflection that they were getting on that committee for the purpose of seeing that the judges' salaries were made adequate to their own brilliant intellects when the time should come for them to occupy this high and dignified position. So I say, appoint your committee, if you wish, but leave the lawyers off it.

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext: On both sides.

Cn both
sides, certainly. I hope that so far as this side is concerned none of them will go on the committee; I do not know but what I would exclude them even from the meetings of the
committee, for fear they might be doing a little lobbying with regard to the bright future that lies before them.
Another thought which I have, and which should be considered by the committee is this: are we going simiply to sit back and have a committee of fifteen appear before parliament and tell us what we ought to do in this matter? I say at once that the judges should be given a remuneration commensurate with the position they occupy, although I am not so terribly impressed with the dignity of their office to the degree that has been expressed almost entirely by lawyers in this discussion; but we will include the dignity too, if you like. But the matter which should be considered by the committee is this, whether you are going to carry with these salary increases a pension for the judges. Personally I am opposed to that. I do not say that because I have anything against the judges personally. I say, make the salaries of the judges fair and reasonable and just, and let them provide for their own old age out of the salaries they receive. I have maintained that position in this house before, and I assert it again. The majority of the fathers of those who sit in this house, I venture to say, did not get any provision made by parliament for a pension for them in their old age. They had to provide for their own old age out of a great deal smaller salary than the judges are getting, and I say that it is up to the judges and everybody else to provide for their old age out of the salaries they receive, and the country should not hand to them on a silver platter, with all the frills around it, both a very fine salary and the assurance that when they get tired of sitting on the bench they can retire on a pension and go into politics, as has been done sometimes in this house in the past.
Like Mr. Doherty.

And D. D.
McKenzie also. Do not forget him when you mention Mr. Doherty. When they tire of the bench, when they find their duties too onerous and too hard upon them and they cannot stand the strain any longer, they resign on a pension of five or six thousand a year, and some of them go into politics. That has happened on both sides of this house, and then when they get tired of politics, when political life becomes too strenuous for them, they go back to the bench, possibly to make provision for another pension when they retire a second time. I protest against that. I say, fix the salaries of the judges at a fair and reasonable figure as compared with similar positions elsewhere, and having regard to

their responsibilities and duties, and let them provide out of their own salaries for their old age, the same as everybody else has to do in this country.

I am aware that this is not the proper time to go in detail into the question of increasing the judges' salaries, yet I wish to make a few remarks. We are being asked to increase the salaries of the judges, some of whom I believe are now receiving in the neighbourhood of ten thousand a year, and I am not sure that some of them are not getting twelve thousand or more a year, and when they retire they receive two-thirds of their salary as a pension. I have a very high opinion of the judiciary of Canada. I would like to see them properly paid, and I am very glad to see that the proposal is that this question shall go before a committee where it can be thoroughly investigated. I have noticed in connection with this resolution, as with others of a similar character, that when a request comes before the house to increase the salaries of the rich it meets with very great favour in some quarters, and any member who dares to dissent is treated with more or less contempt. The Minister of Justice gave as a reason for making this motion that he had received a request from the judges themselves for increased remuneration; but let me remind the house that very persistent requests for better pay have been made by the rural mail carriers. Why is it that the poor, being greater in number, do not receive the same consideration as those who are in receipt of big salaries? I do not say that I would not favour increasing the salaries of some of our lower paid judges, but I think the matter should be very carefully considered before any action is taken. I might point out that in dealing with this matter we are not in the same position as we were when we increased the salaries of ouir deputy ministers. We were in danger of losing their services because of the higheT salaries they were offered by private corporations; but I have not heard of any shortage of applicants for appointment to the bench. As a matter of fact, you find them everywhere. What, then, is the reason for this proposal? Is it because judges are not receiving sufficient remuneration in comparison with thousands of other men who have not one-half, one-quarter, yes, in some cases not one-tenth the income enjoyed by the judiciary to maintain and educate their families? I am very much inclined to oppose increasing the remuneration of our higher paid judges until others who are more needy have their requests for increase of salary dealt with.

I doubt, Mr. Speaker, if I should discuss this motion at all, seeing that the right even of my desk mate (Mr. Woodsworth) was questioned by the hon. member for West Calgary (Mr. Bennett) when he rose to ask for information; but, you know, "fools rush in where angels fear to tread." If he had been a gentleman of less attainments I suppose he would have been treated with contempt by the leader of the opposition. This matter has come before the country during the past six months in various ways, and I think most of us have been circularized by the judges themselves. I wonder why it should be beneath the dignity of any body of men to appear before parliament, since parliament is the highest court in the land. We should maintain our dignity and not think of ourselves as a " rabble". Certainly the member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens) has no right to even hint that the proceedings of the committee itself will be anything more than a wrangle. After reading a despatch in to-day's paper I doubt very much that the dignity of these judges will be hurt by appearing before a committee of this house. Let me quote a short paragraph:
Last year there were 38,000 meals served in the restaurant at a cost of $1.00 per meal. There is now a deficit of $27,000 facing the officials, which includes arrears of $300 from four former members of parliament, and a prominent civil servant. One of the former members is now a Nova Scotia judge.

What paper is the
hon. member reading from?
The Ottawa Journal of today.
If I may be permitted, I should like to state that there is no such deficit facing the restaurant.
Since the judge referred to allows his name to be used in a daily journal in such circumstances, I wonder if it would hurt his dignity very much to appear before a parliamentary committee.
It is a good argument for higher pay, though.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to correct a
statement made by the hon. member for Frontenac-Addington (Mr. Edwards). I want to say to him and to this house that the late Mr. Justice McKenzie did not draw a pension; he died in office. Neither does his widow draw a pension. I do not think it adds to the dignity of our discussion of a matter of such serious importance as this for an hon. member to suggest that a gentle-

As a fellow-Nova Scotian I may say that we are proud of the services that the late Mr. Justice McKenzie rendered to his native land. I for one regret that a pension is not payable to his widow.

Might I
ask the hon. gentleman, would my observation have been less objectionable if the person to whom I referred was still living?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I do not think the question is intended seriously. My hon. friend was endeavouring to find somebody as a horrible example, and there was suggested to him the name of a gentleman who happened to be one of his own political faith. He immediately shifted and suggested the name of the late Air. Justice McKenzie, but the facts show that Mir. Justice McKenzie was not in the class he endeavoured to describe. The late Mr. Justice McKenzie did not draw a pension either as a county court judge or as a supreme court judge.
All I have to say is that my hon. friend should direct his attention first of all to the hon. gentlemen on his own side who introduced the question.

I wish to say a few words on this question, which I think is of paramount importance to the country. It is of great importance because it is vital to the administration of justice that competent and able men should be on the bench, and that they should be enabled to carry themselves in keeping with the dignity of their position. At first I was favourable to the appointment of a committee; that was my first impression: the idea seemed to be sound. But upon reflection it occurred to me that it was not a dignified position for the judges to be placed in, to have them appear before the committee and advocate their request. And if they are not to appear personally then the chief witnesses, the interested parties, are denied presence in the court which is to determine the matter at issue. The Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) and the Solicitor General (Mr. Cannon) failed to tell us what witnesses would appear before the committee or what evidence would be given beyond the facts which are now in the possession of the government or available in the departments.
My real object is to point out that there is not a siingle indication given that any witnesses, apart from the judges or those representing their point of view, could give any evidence that would be of the slightest use beyond such evidence as the parliamentary committee could secure from the Department of Justice or from the formal presentation of the case with respect to applications for increase in salary. I would ask the Minister of Justice this question: Can he conceive of any evidence which might be adduced either equal to or of comparatively the same importance as the evidence of the judges themselves, whose presence before the committee will be denied? Or can he conceive of any witnesses who, if they appeared before the parliamentary committee, could give any information of real and vital importnace to that committee in addition to the facts which are already at his disposal?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I have already spoken, but in answer to my hon. friend I will repeat that the judges of the high courts of Canada have made no application. If any application has been made it has been made by representatives of the bar associations in the various provinces and by the Canadian Bar Association, and surely these people can come and lay their case before the committee.

speakeroldname: Mr. C. H. CAHAN (St. Lawrence-St. George):
speechtext:
I cannot see that the matter which we have before us would be adivanced by referring it to a committee. Who are going to oppose it? Will the government require a recommendation of the whole committee-a unanimous recommendation? Will they act upon the recommendation of a minority or will they act upon the recommendation of the majority? Because a committee of fifteen cannot, I am convinced, be appointed by this house which will represent the general view of the house upon the question. For my part, although I may not be presumed to have much confidence in the committee of fourteen or fifteen who compose the government of Canada at the present time, I have far more confidence in their judgment than in the judgment of any special committee in dealing with a matter of this kind; and if they are prepared in 'the constitutional way to recommend increases in the salaries of judges who are appointed by them, I standi ready to vote for any reasonable measures proposed to that end. And so far as my personal knowledge goes, as regards the majority on this side, they are prepared to assume a similiar attitude. I have no doubt that although there may be differences of opinion on this side of the house, the majority of the members over here would support the government in any reasonable measures it might take to increase existing
Judges' Salaries

salaries so as to give adequate recompense to the judges of the land. I regard this innovation in constitutional practice, which we have before us to-day, not as an effort to deal with the question seriously but really as a method of postponing considleration of it until the Greek Kalends or to some other distant date. I cannot conceive that the government, being anxious to deal with the question in the way of providing adequate recompense for the judges, would have taken the course now proposed. In this matter, as in others, the government must take full responsibility for presenting to the house any measure for the expenditure of public money. There is no reason why they should now prove recreant to the trust which the constitutional practice of the country vests in them. There is no adequate reason why we should1 have a change in the constitutional procedure in the present instance and not in respect of every other vote that is to come before parliament when the estimates are .brought down for consideration. Not a single serious ground can be suggested, it seems to me, why the proposed vote-if there is to be a vote-should come before parliament in any way other than in the estimates which are brought down by the government for the consideration of the house. The present proposal is simply an effort to preclude the serious consideration of the question in the future and to prevent parliament as parliament dealing with it; because we can deal with it pertinently and successfully only when the actual vote is submitted to parliament. I personally believe, despite the differences of opinion which prevail on the other side of the house, despite also some dissent on this side, that if the government would take their courage in their hands and bring down a vote which they might consider sufficient to provide adequately for the judges of the land, a large majority in the house would sustain them. We know that hon. members of the government would deal with such a matter in a perfectly disinterested temper, notwithstanding that some of them may be candidates for judgeships in the future. I will vote against the resolution which proposes to refer this matter to a committee. The result, in my opinion, would be ineffective. This house must decide the question. Every member in this house has now, or would have in the course of the debate here, all the information he would require on which to base a conscientious decision. I therefore regard the remission of this matter to a special committee as an indefinite postponement of its consideration, and for that reason I intend to vote against the motion. At the same time,
[Mr. Cahan.l
I believe that if the government will bring down a measure in the ordinary course, they will find themselves sustained by a large majority in this house, including, as I believe, the large majority of my confreres on this side.

I
agree very largely with the remarks of my hon. friend who has just spoken (Mr. Cahan). So long as the present system obtains, whereby the government controls the preparation of all the estimates, exercising arbitrary powers with respect to every money proposition submitted to the house, the view taken by my hon. friend will be absolutely right. But it does not follow that this or that method should be maintained, or some other practice substituted in its place, simply because it may have been adopted in the United States congress or anywhere else. It seems to me that there is too great a disposition in Canada, in the country at large and in parliament in particular, to say that we should or should not do this or that, merely because it is done in Washington or London or elsewhere. When we have an opportunity to exercise our responsibility for the good of Canada, for heaven?s sake let us do so in our own way. Of course, that does not mean that there are not certain things which we should imitate, but too often we invoke a precedent from across the ocean or from south of the 45th parallel to justify us in doing this, that or the other thing, which displays too much of the subservient colonial spirit still prevailing in this country.
When the rules of debate were subjected to our judgment, upon which I do not think we acted with very much judgment, I suggested one real reform in the management of the affairs of the country, one that would, I think, be conducive to public good, and result in abridging the work of the house, while enabling both the government and the individual members to deal with general matters without being clap-trapped for weeks and months in the consideration of small details. My suggestion was that all the details of the estimates should be submitted to a committee of the house, before which the permanent officials of each department should appear to give that information individually which they now give like schoolboys to their masters from two chairs in front of the minister, while the poor minister must repeat to the committee what he is told by his officials.
Therefore I am going to support this resolution, because I consider it to be the beginning of a new system which may prove to us that many matters connected with the

Judges' Salaries
management of the country could be dealt with more properly, as to their details, their preparation and their presentation, by a small committee where witnesses could appear, where the facts could be exposed and where reasons for or against any expenditure of public money could be given. That committee would report to the house, and the house would pass final judgment upon its findings. I do not say this especially in view of the [DOT] object of this resolution; but I believe this is a start which may bring us to the point where we can get away from the absurd system which we have copied from the British House of Commons. There, however, without changing the letter of the law, they have radically changed the manner of dealing with the budget, and in about one-quarter of the time we devote to the voting of our estimates they adopt a budget ten or fifty times as large as ours, with at least equal efficiency. '
I do not think this is the proper time to go into the question of the "dignity" of the judges; I do not think that dignity will be preserved by mere platitudes, or by putting the judges in such a position that they will not be reached by public opinion or by the scrutiny of public conscience. The dignity of the bench must be sustained by the manner in which the judges exercise their functions, and I do not think their dignity will be placed on any higher level by the fact that we raise their salaries by a few thousand dollars. I do not think the dignity of the bench will be impaired by the fact that the judges, if they find their remuneration insufficient, will be called upon to state frankly and under their own responsibility before a committee of this house why they desire a larger salary, instead of making use of representatives of the bar, who will demonstrate to the judges before whom they plead that they have been to parliament asking that the salaries of the judges be increased. It has been imy experience, during a fairly long life, connected in a rather detached fashion with the bar, that some lawyers find it veTy helpful to plead cases either before parliament or elsewhere for the benefit of the judges; they find that in carrying on their profession they reap very tangible results by the manner in which they are treated by some of the judges. I think it much less dignified for the judges to have a few lawyers petitioning members of parliament to increase their salaries, than for those judges to appear before a committee of this house and state simply, in a dignified fashion, what they desire and why they desire it. Dignity is in the man, not in the procedure; it is in the soul, in the frankness of language and the rectitude of the
mind of every individual, whether he be the King or his representative, a judge, or the humblest servant of this house. Among the papers I have received during the session I have noticed two or three petitions with regard to an increase of salaries, one from the charwomen who clean our rooms and another on behalf of the judges. This latter petition was submitted by proxy, but I do not think the charwomen of this house have sacrificed their dignity as women by petitioning for an increase in their salaries; Neither do I think the judges will sacrifice their dignity, if they really think they need an increase, by appearing before a committee of this house and allowing that committee to consider their case.
Therefore, I see no reason why we should reject the proposal. I agree that if the government are to stick to precedent and continue to walk in the narrow trail in which governments have walked for the last fifty years in presenting estimates to this house, there is no sense in this resolution. The government should take the responsibility for these increases of salaries, as my hon. friend from St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Cahan) has said, just as they take the responsibility for the estimates. We have to take human nature into consideration, of course; I know, as everyone knows, that many members on this side of the house are opposed to increasing the salaries of the judges. On the one hand the government do not want to displease the judges and the laywers, while on the other hand they do not want to displease their friends. All governments have resorted to such expedients, and I am not going to vote against the government because they have taken' this way of escaping the direct responsibility connected with this issue. I give my vote in favour of this resolution, because it is a departure from a custom which may have been quite proper in the past but which is not now adequate for the amount of business done in this house or for the various complicated and technical questions with which parliament is called upon to deal. When you and I, Mr. Speaker, were young members of this house, many matters were dealt with directly by the house which are now considered by various special committees, and therefore I consider this a good departure in the right direction.

Mr. Speaker, I do not intend to detain the house for more than just a few moments. I wish to say a word in favour of this resolution, not that I know anything about judges' salaries, as to whether or not they should be
Judges' Salaries

increased; I am quite willing to leave that question to the proposed committee, but I do welcome this slight departure from our established custom, as the previous speaker has said. I have protested against cabinet government ever since I came into this house, and I shall continue to protest against it until there is more responsibility placed upon parliament. Of course it is easier for the government of the day to entrust a matter of this kind if it is not a popular one to a committee, so that the committee may assume the responsibility which the government is not willing to do. But even so I am glad that there is this departure, if indeed it can be regarded as such, of entrusting a little more power to a committee of this house and a little less power to the cabinet. I trust that this will only be the beginning of a much larger departure in that regard, for I believe it will mean a much better type of government and will give each member of parliament some real reason for being here. I shall be glad to support the motion.

I
should like to say a few words on this question. In the first place the discussion has departed from the question under debate which is the appointment of a committee to decide whether the judges should get an increase in Salary or not. I object to it on this ground: The whole question is one of responsible government. That is the question before this house. If the government has decided and apparently it has-we have listened to the Prime Minister, the Minister of Justice, the Solicitor General, and I think one or two others, taking the attitude that thej'- are favourable to the whole proposition -if the government has decided that the judges should get an increase in salary it seems to me it is the responsibility of this government to take the attitude frankly and openly before this parliament. The hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Bourassa) very often stands up in this house and talks about responsible government, and about the traditions of responsible government in Great Britain. I think when we appoint committees to decide what the government has already decided upon we are getting far away from responsible government in Canada. Now, sir, if you appoint a committee to decide a question of this sort you are going to shift the responsibility from the government to a committee of the house. That is what is happening. There are times and there are questions, questions which the house cannot decide itself without interminable debate, when committees should be appointed, but 
here is a question as to which there is no difficulty in coming to a decision. The house is full of lawyers who are in close touch and contact with the judiciary. Any one of them can stand up here and give ample reason why the salaries of the judiciary should be increased, and I am not saying that out of any disrespect to the distinguished gentlemen on the bench. But because of that very fact, because the Minister of Justice already knows to-day the arguments which should be put forward and the reasons which should be advanced in justification of an increase in salary, I do not think there is any reason why this question should be turned over to a committee of the house. Let the government take the responsibility as a government should do in regard to measures upon which it has made up its mind. If this committee is appointed here is what will happen: Should criticism be advanced later the blame would be placed upon the committee, the whole house will be held to be responsible. But we are supposed to have responsible government and under that system this is what happens: If the government brings forward measures and those measures are not supported by the House of Commons then it goes to the people and the people decide whether that government shall continue to handle the affairs of this country or not. If that course be not followed we do not have responsible government at all. I do believe there are certain matters which could well be dealt with by committees. The estimates submitted to parliament could very well be dealt with by a committee; but here, is a question which could be decided by the house itself probably in the course of an afternoon sitting, or at most an afternoon and an evening, and the whole question settled without submitting it to a committee which will tinker with it for weeks, taking members out of this house where they should be taking part in or listening to the debates. I repeat it is the duty of the government to submit this question to the house and have it decided here.
I have one other observation to make and it is this: The Minister of Justice in presenting the resolution quoted the United States as having adopted this system of deciding about the salaries of judges. That brought back to my mind the speech of the Prime Minister a few days ago in which he twitted me for having quoted United States statistics regarding immigration. He said, " Surely we can stay at home for our figures". I apply the Prime Minister's remark to the present question. Governments in the past have decided

Judges' Salaries
questions of this kind by themselves without the aid of committees. I think the present government should come courageously forward on this question and I think they would be supported by the house. The matter could have been decided in about the same period of time as has been taken up in deciding whether or not we should appoint a committee.
Hon. CHARLES A. DUNNING (Minister of Railways and Canals): I cannot be accused of -being a lover of lawyers; anything I say on this question will not be attributed to that. But we are discussing a very important arm of government. The functions of government are said to be executive, legislative, and judicial, and the resolution deals with the men who are engaged in doing the work of the judicial arm of government. One of the most important factors in connection with that arm of government is that it should be, unlike the other two, completely non-partisan in character, completely above disputations of a party nature. I ask what would be the result as relating to the judicial arm of government if any government came to this house with a proposal relating intimately to judges and their salaries and it were carried on a purely party division, or anything approaching a party division, or if one party-one of the parties in the corner let us say-were, on a question of this sort affecting the judges of the country to be placed in the position of voting against the others? That possibility is to my mind one of the best reasons why a question of this kind should be considered by a committee of the house. That procedure does not relieve the government of responsibility.
Nor parliament.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
Nor parliament, but it
does involve a method of approach to the subject which enables it to be settled, may I say, on a rather higher plane than has characterized some of the discussion which has taken place here this afternoon. I think that is the chief merit of the proposal of the Minister of Justice. I am sure we all have a very high appreciation of the services of the judiciary in this country in the past and it is rather unfair to say-and I have been guilty of saying it I will admit-that there is no reason to worry about judges because there are plenty of applicants for judgeships. That is not fair because there are many of the most eminent lawyers in this country who for the good of the country should be on the bench who have refused appointment. That is not generally known. There are always plenty of candidates for any public office which carries any sort of a salary, and for 56103-97
some that do not carry a salary at all, but that does not necessarily mean that the interests of the country are not to be considered rather than the interests of the individuals occupying positions or of those who may aspire to occupy them. After all our great abject is to have the judicial arm of the government manned with the very best men we can get. But it does strike one as pecuEar to know that a man sitting on the bench as a judge frequently has before him two or three lawyers pleading each of whom is in receipt of an income seven or eight times as large as that of the judge before whom the case is being tried. I know that has no fundamental bearing on the question but it furnishes a comment on the situation. I have no fixed opinion as to whait should be done with regard to the indivdual salaries of judges, but I do think that calm reflection by a committee of the house upon a question so essentially non-partisan as this one, a question upon which a non-partisan decision is above all things to be desired, is to the advantage of the house and the country.

It appears to me that the weakness in the arguments of the hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat (Mr. Dunning), is this: If it is so very important for a non-partisan committee of this house to fix the salaries of judges, how much more important would it be for a committee of this house to appoint the judges? I should Eke to ask the government if it is not a fact that the appointments of all judges in the past have been partisan appointments. There is a story told of a conversation between a Canadian and an American. The Canadian made the remark to the American: In your country the judges have to be elected. The American made the reply: Yes, and I believe that in Canada they first have to be defeated.
What is the basis of this resolution? Is it not simply that the government has trouble in its own ranks regarding the matter and it wants to shift the responsibility on to parliament? If it has not, why are the reasons held back that the government does not assume its responsibility and bring down a measure as it does in connection with every other matter? This is a violation of the regular order of procedure of government. As the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Manion) has rightly said, it is the duty of a government to assume responsibility for its actions. This government is prepared to do that only when the road is easy. When there is any difficulty ahead it wants to make parliament share the responsibility. You will

Judges' Salaries

pardon me, Mr. Speaker, and I hope the house and the country will pardon me if I refuse to be one of those who hold the judiciary of this country in the idolatry in which it is generally held. They are human like everybody else. As I said before, they are mostly political appointees, sometimes of one party and sometimes of another, and the difficulty that I see in this matter is that you are not rewarding men according to the services they perform on the bench, but attaching salaries to positions. Nobody in this house, for example, will say that every man on the bench is equal to every other man in any of the different courts. Is that not something that should be taken into consideration? Should we not also consider the fact that men who go on the bench do not necessarily go there for the money? Do men come into parliament for the money? Do men go into the cabinet for money? Is there not in the case of nearly every member of parliament and of the 'cabinet a financial sacrifice when he takes a position of that kind? Does a man not accept a position in the high courts of Canada for something outside of the monetary consideration? Is it not worth something to him, to his family and to the record that he will leave behind him, to think that he has held a high position in our courts?
I am not opposed to this measure in the least; I think our judges should be paid in proportion to the service they render and to their ability, but there is more to be taken into consideration than simply the monetary award a man receives when he ascends the bench. Many of them are well-off when they accept a position of that kind. Many of them do not need the money. I say this without any disrespect, that there are in this country some minor judges who do not work more than one or two months in the year. Are we going to raise the salaries of them all, or are we simply going to pick out certain courts and raise t'he salaries there, or how is this matter to be handled? It is the duty of the government to formulate its policy, to bring it before parliament and to ask parliament to sanction it. We got the clue to the difficulty from an hon. member on the ' other side when he said that he was opposed to this resolution. It is the trouble in the ranks of the people behind the government and not any principle which is at stake, that has forced the government to come to parliament with this resolution. Consequently,
I for one say that it is the duty of the government to come to parliament with a bill, if IMr. McGibbon.]
they think fit to bring one in to raise the salaries of judges, and to ask parliament to sanction it.

Mr. Speaker, the Solicitor General (Mr. Cannon) said that the cabinet was a committee of parliament. Everyone, including the Solicitor General, knows that is not true. The cabinet is a committee of the Liberal party and nothing else, and because by referring this matter of the salaries of judges to a special committee, we would be referring it to a committee of parliament, I am very much in favour of the resolution brought down by the government.
May I say I was astonished and pained to hear the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) say to the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) that had he been a man of less education, he would have treated his question with the contempt it deserved? I have very much less education and I would have asked the same question. We are in this house as equals- I am not sure that the lawyers will agree with that-we are here to represent the Canadian people, and while I do not mind taking a position which might cause me a loss of dignity personally, because I do not suffer from dignity, I refuse to take a subordinate position for Southeast Grey. The people of my constituency have just as much right to say what they think on any question, and to ask any question they like in the House of Commons, as the people of any other constituency, even though the other constituency be represented by a high light in the legal profession. Therefore I resent what has been said and I think on further consideration the leader of the opposition will be sorry that he made the remark.
I am interested in the question of crime, and I think it would be true to say that if as much consideration was given to the standard of living and to the salaries of people we now know as criminals, or to all the people of Canada, as has been in the past and, I have no doubt, will be in the future given to the salaries of judges, we would need no judges. I am not going to go into the question whether judges need an increase in salary or not, but I can most heartily approve the method the government has taken. They may have done it for reasons of expediency but at least it is a democratic move and I approve the fact that they are sending the question to a committee on which all sections of the house will be represented. I do not think that is asking too much because this is just a class group coming to parliament and asking for an in-

Judges' Salaries
crease in salary, and we have just as much right to pass upon it as members of another group would have supposing we came to them and asked for an increase in salary for our class.

A question arises here

I think in the manufacture of carpets these yarns are retained free under the British preference, but in the manufacture of twine' and cordage they are not. A question of principle arises there. Speaking for myself, I have no objection to reasonable protection being given articles of this kind, but when such protection is imposed it ought to be carried through to the manufactured article. Previously, under item 558, yam was imported free and the twine into which this yam was manufactured carried duties of 20, 224 and 25. Under item 537 yam is made dutiable at 124, 174 and 25, but the protection on the twine made out of that yam remains the same-20, 224 and 25. The spread between the semi-raw material and the finished article1, the rates of which were 20, 224 and 25, is now 54, 5 and nothing. In this instance, as I have pointed out, several very deserving industries in the country, which have been set up under the existing tariff, have been enjoying a measure of protection on their finished product, importing their raw materials under this free item. Now a duty is imposed on their raw materials but no corresponding increase is given them in connection with their finished product. Perhaps the minister can explain these items.

The house resumed from March 19, consideration in committee of Bill No. 14, to incorporate the Niagara Falls Memorial Bridge Company-Mr. Pettit-Mr. Johnston in the chair.
On section 7-Powers.-Construct bridge across Niagara river, etc.

I wish to refer to clause
7,	which deals with the location of this bridge. The clause reads:
The company may construct, maintain and operate a bridge across the Niagara river for the passage of pedestrians, vehicles, carriages, electric cars or street cars and for any other like purpose, with all necessary approaches from a point at or near a point between the property of the Canadian National railways on River road and the north limit of Bender street.
In other words, they may put their bridgehead on the Canadian side from the northern line of the Canadian National Railway property. I have called the attention of the Minister of Railways to this, and it seems to me the government is making a great mistake in proposing to allow a bridge to be built close to that property. The Canadian National Railways have been aided by the park commission to widen out their road for their own convenience; they have brought in their railway tracks there, and to have a bridgehead butting up against their property with the consequent cluttering up and con-

gestion of traffic, is absurd. If the government were to leave this matter of location to the railway board I am quite sure they would never allow a bridge to be placed there; but under this clause, when the matter reaches the railway board, all they can do is to accept the point that we lay out. We say under that clause of the bill that the bridge must be between these two certain points. We do not give the railway board an opportunity to say whether that is the right place or not. We simply tell them the bridge is to go there, although that is no place for a bridge to be. If we were to say instead that this bridge can be placed between a certain point and another a mile away, the railway board would have an opportunity of doing something, but this clause limits them to about eight hundred feet. That is absurd; no government should allow such a thing, and I am surprised that the Minister of Railways or his department has not noticed that clause.

The hon. member for Lincoln, referring to clause 7, says that the railway board would have no right to say where the bridge is to be located. The first part of clause 8 reads:
The said bridge shall be constructed and located under, and be subject to, such regulations as the governor in council prescribes.
Perhaps the Solicitor General might answer this question. Does that mean that the governor in council would determine where the bridge would go?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
There is no doubt about
that.

If that be the case, why does clause 7 not say positively that the bridge shall be between two certain points? In other words the Solicitor General would say that the railway commission can determine at what point between those two points the bridge will be placed. I will agree that they can do that. But the minister will not say that the railway commission could determine the location of the bridge two hundred feet on the other side of Bender street. My complaint is that all that the railway board will be able to do is to determine at what point between the two particular points that are mentioned, the bridge will be located.

On section 12-power to issue shares as paid-up stock in payment of acquired properties.

I simply wish to note that
under this clause the entire stock of the company may be watered. The provision is that the capital stock of the company shall be $1,500,000, divided into shares of $100 each. speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: The cost of getting the charter.

Yes, issued for the cost of

I have done it as a lawyer, and I will do it again-arrange for contracts to pay up capital stock by fictitious values-as long as this parliament authorizes it to be done. I have no moral scruples at all if I am engaged as counsel in organizing a company so long as parliament authorizes it; that is, I will draw contracts which will enable my clients to comply with the law. But sitting as a member of parliament, I say that I do not approve of legislation which enables companies exercising public franchises to water their stock to the full limit, and then provide means for the redemption of that stock for cash as if it had been paid up in cash.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
I am not as familiar with company operations as my hon. friend, not

having had his long experience at the bar. I am quite sure that many abuses could be wiped out, but I do not think his remarks have any relation to clause 12, which authorizes the company to pay for certain things with paid-up shares of their capital stock instead of in cash. The original clause contained the word " services ", which we have deleted. We did so to obviate exactly what my hon. friend has mentioned. As the clause reads now the paid-up shares can be given only in payment for any businesses, franchises, undertakings, rights, powers, privileges, and so on.

My objection is that the deletion of the word " services " leaves it wide open still. No counsel called upon to organize this company need exercise his imagination if he wishes to find either a business, or a franchise, or an undertaking, or a right, or a privilege, or some letters patent, or some invention, or some real estate, or some stock, or an asset, or some other property, which he can place in the contract as the consideration for the issue of the $1,500,000 of capital stock. There is no provision in this section and no provision under the general law which would enable a court to investigate and ascertain whether or not that consideration was of real value to the amount of the stock issued. That is my objection. I am simply calling attention to the present practice, so that the Solicitor General may act with his eyes wide open. I think the time has come when we should be very careful in authorizing these corporations exercising public franchises to issue their stock for a mere nominal value.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: The abuse exists in the general practice covering all these companies. This is no exception.
It is no exception at all.
Why make it possible to do so in this case?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
The underlying principle
of all legislation is that people are supposed to do what is right. People may take hold of a clause passed in entire good faith by this parliament and make a use of it that none of us could foresee; but if we attempt to legislate with that object in view we will never be able to frame clauses to meet all the eventualities which may be brought about by the ingenious brains of modern finance.

If the promoters of this company exercise the rights which parliament has created and bestowed upon them, I recognize no moral wrong in their so doing. I am

simply calling attention to the fact that these companies do it when authorized by law-as this company will be-and they do not regard themselves as abusing the law or as proceeding in any immoral manner whatsoever; nor do I. But we as trustees in this parliament are doing wrong, for we are creating the opportunity for abuse of the public franchises which we bestow upon such companies.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: This clause does not give anybody a legal right to do wrong.
Because it is not wrong.
How could they do wrong if they act under a legal right?

speechtext: The clause gives power to the company to pay with paid-up stock, something which is worth while.

Certainly. The clause

The directors may issue as paid-up stock shares of the capital stock of the company in payment for any businesses,
And so 6n. But if those directors meet and decide to give their paid-up stock for something which is not worth anything, we are not conferring such a right upon them.
You are giving them legal authority to do it.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: They would be simply interpreting the clause in a sense altogether foreign to what it means.
This clause authorizes the transfer of $1,500,000, the entire capital stock of the corporation, for a patent or invention.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: Which is worth something.

For something which may have no actual value above $100 in cash, and we with our eyes open are authorizing the company to do that. When we once give such authority by statute it is no immoral act, so far as my conviction goes, if the promoters should exercise their. statutory rights to the full extent.
Mr. Chairman, I want to assure hon. members that the water will run under the bridge and not through it.

By this section, Mr. Chairman, we are authorizing the directors to issue $1,500,000 worth of stock. We have an interest in the value of that stock, because the company hold out to us the prospect of this bridge being returned to us. Therefore we ought to put some value on the stock so as
to know what it is going to cost us should we take over the bridge. I mentioned this more than once before the committee, but no notice was taken. I wish to enforce my point; so long as I am a member I intend to do likewise in respect of any legislation of this kind. I have experience in this sort of thing. If the committee is prepared to approve of what I consider an improper provision, then it will do so with its eyes open. Section 18 provides:
When the corporate obligations of the company and of any of the companies mentioned in sections 14, 15 and 10 of this act, with which this company shall join or unite in the construction of said bridge, shall have been paid-
So far this provision is reasonable, if these corporate obligations are issued at a proper price. But the section proceeds:
-and their capital stock shall have been retired in the manner prescribed in their by-laws

The capital stock of $1,500,000 may be issued for a patent right worth $100, and then the by-laws may provide that that stock, of which $1,500,000 has been issued for a real value of $100, may be retired at any price mentioned therein. That is what the section means. So that if the by-law which is passed by the directors of the company, and approved in due course by the shareholders, so provides, this stock of $100 par value, for which less than 1 cent has been paid in actual cash value, may be retired, not at $100 even, but at $200, $300, $400 or at any price they choose. I suggest that in the incorporation of companies exercising public franchises such as this we should direct attention to provisions of this nature. We should consider them with our eyes open and not approve so readily of a section such as this.

It is quite true that there

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: In respect of their capital stock.

If the tolls are sufficiently
high to pay, say, 12 per cent upon every share of $100 par value issued, the stock will sell in the market at say twice par; and if the stock is selling in the market-its nominal value being $100-at two or three hundred dollars, and the shareholders come to this government, or to a Conservative government, these people who have bought and paid for their stock at this heavy premium will be allowed, under the by-laws of the company, to receive reimbursement on that basis. The difficulty is this: The promotor who procures the issue of $1,500,000 of stock for a consideration worth $100 in real value, or even $1,000, does not continue to own the stock; he is a stock speculator. He puts the stock out on the market and there is turnover after turnover until the stock reaches a premium of perhaps two or three hundred per cent. When the stock is finally transferred to the possession of the shareholder who has paid two or three hundred per cent premium, and when that shareholder comes to the government and asks for the approval of a by-law m respect of its redemption, the government will be in fact morally bound not to deprive him of the property for which he has paid full value. The promoter, however, has put one and a half millions or more into his pocket as a result of the transaction. In my judgment, these public utility companies exercising public franchise, whether they be tramway or railway companies, should not be allowed to issue their stock except for actual cash value, because they are exercising a public franchise, and their tolls should be kept in such ratio or proportion as will enable them to earn an income or dividend of a reasonable rate per cent upon the actual cash which has gone into the enterprise. It is different altogether from an ordinary industrial company, which is not speculative in this sense. They should be kept rigidly down within the usual limitations and restrictions imposed upon companies exercising a public franchise.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall the preamble be adopted?

Before the preamble carries I should like to say a word on the principle embodied in this bill. You are giving power in this bill to a private company to construct a public utility. This bridge is to be constructed over the Niagara river,, and no doubt in the future it will become very valuable to the company which owns it. To my thinking private ownership of a public utility is always an evil. We have found that out in the west, and sooner or later the government, or parliament, or the public themselves, have to deal with the situation thus created. We in the west have found that it has been necessary to take over practically every public utility with which we have had to do since settlement started in that country. There is some difference in eastern Canada and western Canada regarding public utilities. The idea in connection with a public utility is that all the work shall be done at cost. It seems that in eastern Canada, owing to protective privileges, it is possible to pass on the cost ultimately to a portion of the

Ways and Means-Customs Tariff
community that has no means of obtaining relief from the burden. This bill grants to a company a charter which I believe is being secured for the purposes of trading. It is a piece of legislation which gives power to the company to do a great deal of charter mongering. I have more than a suspicion, by the way, that certain clauses of this bill will permit this company to amalgamate with other companies, and that the charter is being secured for no other purpose than to rake in the dollars.
Carried.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order.

Levity is all very well, gentlemen, but this legislation is too serious to go through without a good deal of thought, and I am surprised to see men representing constituencies in the west sitting down and taking this thing so coolly. Whether this enterprise is to be located in eastern Canada or in the west the matter is one which affects the whole nation. It is in reality a national affair, and I feel that the putting of this great public utility in private hands is an evil that will be felt more and more in the years to corpe. When this measure came up in the committee on railways and canals last year I opposed it on the ground that it was a public utility which should never be allowed to go into private hands. It is international in its character, and if it is needed the two nations concerned should carry out the work. It should be done as the result of a joint agreement between the two countries, just as is proposed in the case of the St. Lawrence deep waterway. It can only be carried1 out as the result of a definite plan carefully studied in advance. It is certainly in the interests of the whole of Canada that the granting of charters of this kind to private companies-
Carried.
-for the sake of gain should be stopped.
Carried.
