The time has come in
Canada when we should think in a national sense in regard to the question of wool. I know that a year ago, when this matter was spoken of, the Minister of Finance took objection to the placing of a dulty on wool, under a misconception, I believe. I am not going to discuss this matter simply from the standpoint of the tariff or the effect the tariff may have upon the woollen industry.
This country to-day is suffering from a lack of sheep, and to a greater extent than probably any of us imagine. From time immemorial the flocks and the herds and the soil have been the three primitive assets of every nation. We stand to-night in the face of certain remarkable facts which I want to mention, and the first is this: Canada has less sheep per head of population than any other country on the face of the earth. There must be some reason for this. In 1911 the government of Sir Wilfrid Laurier appointed a gentleman from my constituency, Mr. Dryden, a great breeder of sheep and probably one of the best experts on sheep in this country, to investigate the industry.	He went to the United States
and England investigating the industry, and came back in 1912 and made his report to parliament. This report has never been acted upon, has never even been seriously considered by parliament. He points out in this report, m the first place, that a country must have sheep, that they are a fundamental necessity. We speak of combating noxious weeds by means of chemical compounds, but it is absurd to expect anyone to go to a laboratory and mix up a concoction of arsenic and calcium, and expect by such means to get rid of noxious weeds. Sheep is the natural scavenger of the soil, and anyone who has been through our section of the country and chased home a flock of sheep knows that he will never find a dirty farm where a flock of sheep is kept. Twenty-five or thirty sheep will keep the farm clean; that is a common observation. Next, that farm will be a fertilized farm. Sometimes we do not realize what is taking place in this country. Take the automobile, for instance, and how it is displacing the horse. I am not going to talk against the automobile, but if the number

of horses per head of population in Toronto in 1891 were maintained at the same rate to-day, Toronto would require 60.000 horses to carry on local transportation in that city. As a matter of fact, it has only 3,000 horses, and the same condition applies in all our cities and towns. It is simply beyond figures to estimate the value of the fertilization obtained from a source of that kind. We think we can supply this natural fertilization of our soil by artificial means, but this I claim is only an experiment; nobody knows whether or not artificial fertilization is going to last in our oountry. We do know, however, that in certain valleys in Asia and China where they have always resorted to natural fertilizers the soil is just as fertile to-day as it was two thousand years ago. Now I find that we have not as many sheep as we had even twenty-five or thirty years ago, simply because we are paying no attention to the development of our flocks and herds. I regard this as an extremely important matter.
Sometimes I have been asked how many sheep we have in Canada. We should have at least ten million; as a matter of fact we have only two million. There is no reason in the world why we should not have at least ten million sheep. Mr. Dryden and other stock men in my riding-and I claim that many of the best authorities on sheep and other live stock reside there-advise me that we can raise as good sheep in Canada as in any other country in the world. Proof of this is to be found in the fact that when we exhibit our sheep at the great stock shows they are awarded all the prizes. I am also advised that the wool is of just as good quality as that grown in Australia and other wool-producing countries. But we pay no attention to this question, although it is fundamental. We allow mohair to be imported free of duty. I am not quarrelling with that, for this reason:	We consume
$15,000,000 worth of mohair every year. Mohair is the fleece of the little angora goat. I have only seen one of these goats in Canada. I have been endeavouring to get some wealthy men to establish an angora goat farm in order to teach our people that in these little animals there is a source of great wealth. The farmers of South Africa raise immense flocks of angora goats on their waste land, and reap fortunes from the wool crop. The place from which to get those goats is in the Angora valley of Turkey. While making investigations as to where the best quality of angora goats are bred, I ascertained that the Turkish government regard the angora goat industry of such value to their people that they prohibit the sale and export of any of these animals.
Between this city and my home in Oshawa is sufficient waste land to accommodate all the angora goats needed to supply our market with mohair. Seventy million pounds of wool are required by our people every year, yet we grow only fifteen million pounds, and half of that we export to another country for weaving. This should be investigated. The very best market in the world for wool is to be found in Canada, and yet we go to no trouble to develop sheep and goat breeding to supply this market, largely because of defects in our ideas and in our government.
I am not speaking of this government particularly. It would take ten years of concerted' action to bring about a transformation in this respect. In the first place the government should impose a small tariff on all wool, just to establish the principle, and raise it each year for ten years, and so protect the market of Canada for those of our people who would go into this business.
I wrote to one hundred of our best sheep raisers in Ontario for their opinion as to the best lines on which to develop this industry.
I asked them if they thought it would be of service to the country to standardize prices, so that a farmer for the next ten years would know what return he would get for his wool.
I believe it would be an excellent policy for the government to take into consideration at this very moment. There are many phases of this question to be attacked, and they should be attacked in an intelligent way. One of our best known farmers said to me within the last two months. "Sheep are the most profitable thing I have on my farm to-day. They give me at least two crops a year, one of wool and the other of lambs. I say it is the business of the government to consider what should be done. We should appoint a board or commission to deal with this question in order that our farmers may be encouraged to go into the raising of sheep and goats to provide wool for the Canadian market. I have estimated that to raise sufficient sheep to provide our own requirements for wool would create a living for 72,000 people. Right at our door we have the market means of developing this industry for our farmers.
I feel very strongly about this thing. I have gone to considerable trouble to investigate the facts, and in my opinion it is our business to proceed to develop our flocks and herds as one of our best assets. Ten million sheep would add to the assets of Canada 200 million dollars. It is not merely a matter of tariff. We should deal with each phase of this question as it comes up, and aim at get-' ting within the next ten or fifteen years at least ten million sheep in Canada.

I would like to say a word or two in regard to this question of wool. I am very glad indeed to see the hon. member showing so much solicitude for the farmers and sheep growers, but I would like to remind the house that wool is not the only feature of the sheep industry. The sale of lambs plays a very important part, and many of us have thought that the larger market in the United States which would have been provided by the reciprocity treaty would have greatly helped that feature of the industry.
Does the hon. member know that he had that market, and that the United States barred him from it?

I know that very well, and I also know that we might have had it a great many years sooner if we had entered into that treaty. There is another very im-

portant feature to be considered, and if any hon. member is anxious to encourage the sheep industry especially in the western provinces I should like to enlist his sympathies in having woven wire fencing placed on the free list. There is nothing which handicaps us more in the west in the raising of sheep than does the cost of fencing. So you cannot consider this question only from the one angle.
With regard to the market for our wool, as I read the trade figures I believe we are getting the full market price for Canadian wool, or at least that we are able to sell to the Canadian trade all that can be absorbed at the present time. Not only that, but I have here the figures of Canada's trade for the six months ending in September, 1927, which show that in that period we sold to the United States 5,860,301 pounds of raw wool having a value of $1,595,801. That wool sold for 27 cents per pound. We imported wool also; during the same six months period our importation of raw wool, camel wool, alpaca wool and goat wool amounted to 5,450,020 pounds, with a value of $1,900,066, while from Australia we imported 204,278 pounds, having a total value of $91,442. That wool was bought at 45 cents per pound, and the very fact of that difference in the price per pound indicates that there is a reason for that trade. What benefit would it be to Canadian manufacturers of woollen goods if we placed an increased duty on that imported wool and compelled them to pay a higher price for their raw product? What advantage would such a duty be to the Canadian farmer who has not got that particular quality of wool to sell? Now those figures surely have some significance. The very fact that we import that quantity of wool from abroad indicates that wool is needed by our Canadian manufacturers.
Will my hon. friend say that wool could not be grown in this country?

Evidently it is not being
grown.
" Evidently " is no argument.
Very well, it is not being grown-
But it could be.
-and the judgment of the men versed in the business is that that particular quality of wool could not be grown-
No such thing.

-in Canada. But I am reminded of a conversation that is supposed to

have taken place between a Scotch shopkeeper and a customer. You have to understand broad Scotch to appreciate it, but the conversation was in these terms:
Customer: Oo?
Shopkeeper: Ay, oo.
Customer: A'oo?
Shopkeeper: Ay, a'oo.
Customer: A'ae oo?
Shopkeeper: Ay, a'ae oo.
That means that the question was not only was it wool, but it was all the same kind of wool. Now this question of wool cannot be considered by thinking of wool all in one class. There is wool and wool, and there is a particular class of wool that is being imported for the benefit of the manufacturers. We do not want to hurt them in this matter, and the putting of a duty on this wool would not be an atom of protection to the Canadian farmer, because the export market in the United States fixes the price for the wool that is used in our Canadian industry.
You cannot convince the Canadian farmer that you are taking proper care of him.

I should like to add one or two words further. First of all. I should not like to have my hon. friend (Mr. Brown) get too badly mixed up in some of his figures. Some five million pounds of Canadian wool are exported, and that woo! is exported to the United States. You may ask yourself the question, " Why is that?". Did the hon. member for Lisgar ever go to any of the leading exporters of wool and ask them some questions concerning this?-
No, he never did.
Well I have done so, and they told me this-

The hon. member for
Lisgar might learn something if he did that.

They told me that one of the' great difficulties about the wool business in Canada is that we have scarcely any men in this country trained to grade wool. I have been told by these men that if our large industries-ns they will do sometimes-need
100,000	pounds of wool of a certain class and a certain grade, it is convenient for them to buy it in tremendous quantities. Unfortunately for us our people have never been trained to grade wool in the way those manufacturers require. Now these men tell me there are factories in the United States that can use one wool, no matter whether it is 56103-99
graded or not, for the purpose of making large quantities of rough blankets and Indian ware where grading is not required, and that is the reason they export their ungraded wool to the United States. What I want to get at is this: The men who know about sheep-and I claim that I have been associated with men in my county who are regarded as authorities on sheep not only in Canada but in the United States and in every other country-tell me, and I am inclined to believe it, that we can grow any kind of wool in Canada that can be grown anywhere else in the world and of as good quality, and that we have a market right at our door. But we require government assistance and government leadership in order that the fleece should be brought to certain centres in each province and men taught there how to grade and handle the wool. If we had a school of this kind we would be able in a few years in Canada to meet the requirements of this country with our own wool produced from our own sheep, and in that way help the Canadian farmer. I am satisfied that if my hon. friend from Lisgar would get in touch with the men who are authorities on this question he would change his mind in a great many respects. We have the best market for wool in the world. Our people use more wool per head than the people of any country on the face of the earth. We have the soil for raising the sheep, and we have the dheep that can produce the wool, but it will require concerted action and leadership on the part of the government, in co-operation with the stock raisers. When we secure that we shall be able to accomplish results in Canada equal to those achieved in Australia, New Zealand, or any other country that has faced this problem.
